models.best: Inferred from its principle that gifts create obligations to give and return, exchange builds trust, alliances and status without relying on price.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that obligations to return a gift can bind people into lasting dependence on whoever gives first, and status can be won by giving more than others can repay. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift; Sahlins, Stone Age Economics (1972)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a family farm which balances its work against household needs keeps output matched to consumption rather than to profit.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a household that stops work once its needs are met may under-invest in tools, land and skills, so output stays low when households are poor or cannot borrow. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central store of goods can feed workers and officials in lean years and fund large public works such as temples and palaces.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that goods collected as tribute are allocated by officials rather than by need or market prices, so storage and pay depend on the central authority's own accounts and loyalty. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that owners who control a fixed labour force can plan planting, harvests and sales over many seasons.
models.worst: The first enslaved Africans in English North America shows how ownership of workers took hold: about twenty captives from present-day Angola came ashore at Old Point Comfort, and planters gained a workforce they could own outright and pass to heirs. Full chattel bondage took decades to form. Sources differ on the ships and captors, and the tobacco link is probable, not certain. Source: Encyclopedia Virginia, Africans in Virginia's first (1619) entry; City of Hampton, The 1619 Landing: Virginia's first Africans

models.best: Inferred from its principle that lords provide land, protection and justice in return for labour, so each manor can supply most of its own food and needs.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour services and rents are owed whatever the harvest, so peasants may keep little surplus in bad years and little reason to improve the land. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society (1939-1940)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that statutes on entry, training and quality give apprentices a clear path to mastery and protect buyers from poor work.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that control of entry and prices can keep newcomers out and raise prices, so skilled trades change slowly. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Epstein, Freedom and Growth (2000)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a state regulating production and trade toward a surplus can build reserves of bullion and secure markets for domestic producers.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that controls on trade and production can protect favoured sectors and colonies at the cost of consumers and rival producers. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Heckscher, Mercantilism (1935)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that one tax on land rent funds the state without taxing labour or trade, and free grain trade keeps food supplies responsive to prices.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a tax on rent alone can leave the state short of revenue when rents are low, and an emphasis on agriculture can neglect manufacturing and services. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy (1962)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competition, secure property and the division of labour let producers specialise and trade, so output can grow as they do.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a state which only protects property and contracts leaves markets without remedies against monopoly or reckless lending, so concentrated firms and financial failures can persist. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Smith, The Wealth of Nations

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, so decentralised price signals can guide production better than a planner can.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit expansion sends false price signals, so a banking system that lets credit grow without limit can produce booms followed by busts. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society (1945)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that steady money growth, open trade and competition can keep prices predictable and give firms a stable base for investment.
models.worst: Chile's Chicago-trained economists and the 1982 collapse: eight banks and finance firms failed in November 1981, output fell about 15 per cent by 1982, and the peso fell 18 per cent and then 55 per cent under a free-float decree. Critics blame the reforms from 1973 for mass unemployment and sharper inequality; defenders point to stable growth. The unemployment figures are not in the results, and the causes are contested. Source: Christian Science Monitor, Chile's economy and the Chicago Boys (21 December 1982); online encyclopaedia (secondary), Crisis of 1982 (secondary); review of Sebastian Edwards, The Chile Project

models.best: Inferred from its principle that spending and taxes that rise in slumps and fall in booms keep demand and employment steady over the business cycle.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that spending that is not reversed in good times can build up debt and inflation, so employment gains may come with rising prices. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Beveridge, Social Insurance and Allied Services (1942)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competition inside a legal order that curbs monopoly, with social insurance and worker representation in firms, can combine growth with protection against market failure.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a legal order that curbs monopoly can be captured by large firms, and social insurance can grow without a link to what it costs, so the market is weakened. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft; Erhard, Wohlstand für Alle (1957)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that universal public services and active labour-market policy, paid for by high taxes, can help people move between jobs while unions bargain wages nationally.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that high taxes and national wage bargaining can slow adjustment when an industry declines, and public services can grow faster than the tax base that funds them. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Saltsjöbaden Agreement; Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism (1990)

models.best: Singapore's public housing (HDB flats) shows a state building homes for most residents, although sources give the share differently for residents and households, so SingStat figures are needed for any number.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit for chosen industries must be disciplined by export performance, so favoured firms that fail to export can keep support and draw resources from others. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle (1982); Amsden, Asia's Next Giant (1989)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a tax on the value of land falls on rent rather than on wages and capital, so it can raise public revenue without taxing labour and investment.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a land tax is hard to value and collect, so landowners can keep gains if assessments lag and speculation may fall less than expected. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities built by example can test new ways of organising work and share gains among members.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities built by example depend on voluntary membership and the commitment of their founders, so they can dissolve when leaders leave or funds run out. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Owen (1813); Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel (1829)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit at cost and free contracts let workers keep most of the value they add, and rent on property is removed.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit at cost depends on trust among members and rules for default, so lending can stall when members cannot repay. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Yugoslavia's workers' self-management gave workers' councils wide powers over output and finance inside a state plan, a form of shared control of firms; the evidence on productivity and wages is thin.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that members who own and control a firm may vote against closures or hard investment, so weak firms can be kept going and losses carried. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mondragón cooperatives (from 1956)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods shared by need within federated communes can meet basic needs without wages, and free association can replace contracts.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that sharing by need gives no price signal of what is scarce, so shortages and waste can arise unless communes coordinate supply. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' organisations running industry directly can give workers a voice over work and output.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that strikes can halt output in disputes, and a general strike could stop the whole economy, so investment may be held back during conflicts. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the French CGT; Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail (1902)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that democratic, gradual public enterprise and a national minimum of welfare can provide basic services without revolution.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that municipal and national public enterprise can grow without tests of firm performance, so monopolies may persist and costs may rise without competition. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the Fabian Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers sharing control through guild-like councils can align production with the needs of those who work and buy.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that several councils sharing control can deadlock, and the state as one partner may dominate or decide slowly. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole

models.best: Inferred from its principle that central plans setting output, prices and investment, with labour mobilised, can concentrate resources quickly on heavy industry.
models.worst: Shortage in the socialist economies (Kornai) describes shortages that are frequent, severe and long-lasting, across consumer goods, housing and producer inputs. Kornai traced them to the soft budget constraint, under which state enterprises faced no hard financial limit and losses did not force closures. A critic argues that soft budgets do not explain most excess demand; the official preference for fast growth does. Source: Kornai, Resource-constrained versus demand-constrained systems, Econometrica (1979); Kornai, Economics of Shortage (1980)

models.best: Hungary's New Economic Mechanism judged firms by profit rather than plan fulfilment and steered them by indirect means; early results were encouraging, with shoppers having more goods and unsold stock falling. The case gives no output figures and rests mostly on abstracts.
models.worst: Yugoslavia's workers' self-management gave workers' councils wide powers over output and finance, but state-appointed executives could still block their decisions. The evidence on productivity, wages and unemployment is thin. Source: Yugoslav pamphlet on self-management (Belgrade, 1950), Marxists Internet Archive; CIA, Yugoslavia: Twenty Years of Self-Management

models.best: Inferred from its principle that once classes disappear, distribution by ability and need can meet basic needs without wages or markets.
models.worst: Shortage in the socialist economies (Kornai) describes shortages in socialist economies as frequent, severe and long-lasting, and traces part of them to soft budget constraints. A critic argues that soft budgets do not explain most excess demand. Source: Kornai, Resource-constrained versus demand-constrained systems, Econometrica (1979)

models.best: Hungary's New Economic Mechanism judged firms by profit and steered them by indirect means; early results were encouraging, but the case gives no output figures and rests mostly on abstracts.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that gradual price reform under party direction, with special economic zones, can leave firms and officials bargaining over allocations, so regions and sectors may develop unevenly. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Naughton, The Chinese Economy (2007)

models.best: Yugoslavia's workers' self-management gave workers' councils wide powers over output and finance, a precedent for councils that plan with workers' voice; the evidence on productivity, wages and unemployment is thin.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that repeated proposal rounds among councils can be slow, and balancing jobs by complexity may leave some work less attractive to those with fewer skills. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward

models.best: Inferred from its principle that organising employers and unions into state-controlled corporations can coordinate investment, training and wage rules across an industry.
models.worst: Germany's employment policy and the Four-Year Plan, 1933 to 1939 is a weak case: its sources are exam-preparation material and its baselines are disputed. It describes armaments rising sharply while consumer goods were short under a plan for self-sufficiency. Do not quote figures from it without an academic source. Source: Secondary study guides (Cognito, Save My Exams, Seneca Learning); to be replaced by an academic economic history before use

models.best: Inferred from its principle that profit-and-loss sharing and a ban on interest can tie finance to real output and risk, while zakat redistributes wealth.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a ban on interest and reliance on trust can make credit harder to price and enforce, so finance may be scarce or slow for borrowers without collateral. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System (1985)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that moderate consumption and small-scale, local production can serve well-being and limit strain on people and resources.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that small-scale production may give up scale economies and specialisation, so some goods may cost more or be harder to obtain. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful (1973)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that widespread private property, small enterprise and a just wage can spread economic power and keep decisions with the smallest competent body.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that small enterprises may lack the capital for large investment or export markets, so some goods may cost more and growth may be slower. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Belloc, The Servile State (1912)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that activity within planetary limits and a social floor under everyone can meet basic needs without a growth imperative.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a fixed scale of activity can leave some regions and workers with lower incomes and less room for new jobs, and debt may rise if output falls. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Daly; Raworth, Doughnut Economics (2017)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that an unconditional income paid to every citizen can cushion risk and support work and care, funded by taxes on land and natural resources.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that an unconditional payment to all can cost a large share of national output, and if it is funded by borrowing it may add to inflation. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All (1995)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government issuing its own currency can fund full employment, with inflation rather than debt as the main limit.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that spending financed by money creation can push up prices once the economy is near full capacity, so a government that ignores inflation can lose price stability. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton

models.best: Inferred from its principle that communities who design, monitor and enforce their own rules can manage a shared resource without either a market or a central planner.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that locally made rules can exclude outsiders or fail to protect resources that span many communities, so wider institutions are needed. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom

compromise.summary: A plural economy: competitive markets under anti-monopoly law, public services and social insurance, worker and member voice in firms, user-owned banks and shops, steady money, a basic floor of income, and shared resources governed by their users. Each form keeps its best practice and is blocked from its worst.
compromise.details: Keeps: indirect steering of profit-based firms, from Hungary's New Economic Mechanism (Market socialism); worker councils with wide powers, from Yugoslavia's workers' self-management (Cooperative economy, Participatory economics); anti-monopoly law and social insurance (Social market economy, inferred); shared resources run by their users (Commons governance, inferred). Blocks: shortages from soft budgets, by hard budget limits for state firms (Shortage in the socialist economies (Kornai)); managers overriding councils, by binding council decisions in law (Yugoslavia's workers' self-management); bank failures after fast deregulation, by prudential supervision and no currency peg (Chile's Chicago-trained economists and the 1982 collapse); owning people, by a legal ban (The first enslaved Africans in English North America). Test: measure unemployment, output, inflation, shortages, bank failures and inequality in pilot regions against comparison regions, over one business cycle. Source: Yugoslav pamphlet on self-management (Belgrade, 1950), Marxists Internet Archive; Kornai, Resource-constrained versus demand-constrained systems, Econometrica (1979); Christian Science Monitor, Chile's economy and the Chicago Boys (21 December 1982); World Politics, Hungarian economic reform (1973); inferred principles: Ostrom, Van Parijs, Müller-Armack.
